ma_joe_s_rock.blurb: A small granite cliff in a conservation parcel in Wrentham, just inside the Rhode Island line. Most of the 14 climbs here are set up as top-ropes from trees or anchors well back from the edge, with a handful of trad lines. Grades start around 5.3 and stretch to 5.12, though the bulk sit near 5.8 and 5.9. The face is steep and technical, with roof moves on several lines, and the rock is mossy and loose in spots, so check holds and anchors before trusting them. Bring long slings or static line for rigging. A short trail from the lot leads to the base, which makes it a quick local session rather than a destination.

ma_foundation_boulder.blurb: A big glacial erratic on Bannon Hill in the Burlington Landlocked Forest, sitting right beside the loop trail near the ruins of an old homestead. All four sides have problems, 14 in total, running from V1 to V4 with most in the V2 to V3 range. Topouts are around ten feet and it is not a highball. An easy downclimb makes it friendly for beginners, while the harder faces give stronger climbers something to work. Expect mountain bikers and dog walkers on the surrounding trails; this is a single-boulder stop, ideal for an hour or two.
ma_foundation_boulder.parking_note: Leave the car in the Turning Mill Road lot.
ma_foundation_boulder.approach: Walk up the power-line trail from the parking for about 0.8 miles, roughly ten minutes, then turn onto the yellow Bannon Hill loop at the second right. Bear left at the fork and follow the yellow and blue markers a few minutes; the boulder is beside the trail just after it switchbacks downhill.

ma_nauset_middleschool_boulder.blurb: A single boulder on the grounds of the Nauset middle school in Orleans, on outer Cape Cod, where boulders are scarce. It packs in 14 problems from around V0 to V5, with the middle of the range, V3 and V4, best represented. The stone is sharp on skin, a graffiti wall covers one side, and broken glass tends to collect below the main face, so bring a brush and a bag. Some problems are about twelve feet tall and the traverse area calls for two crash pads. The block can be seen from the parking area near the soccer fields, so there is almost no walk.

ma_f_wall.blurb: One of the faces around the old Little Railroad Quarry at Quincy Quarries, just south of Boston, and the longest, slabbiest stretch of granite in the quarry. Its trademark is a hanging low-angle slab that makes the wall easy to pick out. Thirteen single-pitch lines, mostly top-rope with some trad, run from about 5.3 to 5.8, so it suits beginners, kids and anyone wanting friction practice. The rock can be friable, especially on the slab, and a 60 m rope may be needed to reach the anchors from the base for top-roping.

ma_r_wall_aka_p_face.blurb: A small craglet at Quincy Quarries, and the first one reached from the main parking area. It is a short, low-angle slab, roughly 30 to 40 feet, covered in old paint and graffiti. The 13 routes are mostly top-ropes with a few trad lines, from very easy terrain up to a single 5.9, with the bulk in the 5.3 to 5.7 band. Most start on the left side of the face. The climbing is plain and unremarkable, but it is a handy spot for newcomers and for working on friction technique on granite.

ma_goose_cove_reservoir_boulders_western.blurb: A scattering of boulders on the west shore of Goose Cove Reservoir in Dogtown, the wooded interior of Cape Ann near Gloucester. About thirteen problems are logged here, from V2 up to a lone V8, with most landing between V3 and V6. Some are tall: one sit-start V3 climbs a twelve-foot overhanging arete of fine-grained granite. The subarea is sunny and reached on foot, so expect a woods walk rather than a roadside stop, and bring pads for uneven ground. A good outing for climbers at the V3 to V6 level.

ma_j_wall_aka_l_face.blurb: A single-pitch face at Quincy Quarries next to the Granite Rail Quarry, left of the striking prow of M Face. Of its 13 lines, almost all are top-rope with one trad route, and routes are around 25 to 50 feet. Grades run from about 5.5 through the 5.10s to a single 5.12, so it has more to offer intermediate climbers than most of its neighbours. The rock is granite with thin face moves and cracks, but loose material sits above the cliff, and ring anchors set back from the edge let you rig top-ropes from the top.

ma_main_alcove_wall.blurb: The steepest and best-known rock in the Hammond Pond reservation on the Newton and Chestnut Hill line near Boston, and the biggest wall in the Alcove Area with 13 problems. Most are traverses or short steep lines from VB to V5, with a pair of far harder test pieces. Heights reach about 15 feet, and past accidents mean landings deserve attention, so bring pads and a spotter. The conglomerate here is overhanging and often chalked, which makes the wall easy to spot. It is a short walk uphill from the parking lot.
